_doc: GENERATED by scripts/native/gen-speak.mjs – see docs/specs/native-m4-vectors.md (P07). Top level = web route (speak, speaking, pron, say, reflex, rtype, roleplay, handsfree) + shared + persist + data. Each case: id, why, input, out. Text inside out is the Vietnamese i18n KEY as the web passes it to t() (a key with variables is {k, v}); map keys through native/shared/strings.json speak.* ids. Microphone/ASR/recording/speech/audio/timers are PLATFORM inputs recorded in each case `input` (heard text, alternatives, error codes, elapsed ms, random numbers); the scoring code that consumes them is the real web code.

recognize._doc: Platform ASR → what the screens get ({ heard, score, alts }): the browser returns up to 5 alternatives; ui.js recognize() keeps the alternative with the highest similarity to the TARGET (ties: first), score = round(similarity·100). similarity = 1 − Levenshtein/maxLen on lower-cased text with everything outside [a-z ] removed (the same function as lesson.json similarity; every (heard,target) pair that also exists there must give the same score). Whisper-on-device returns ONE transcript and uses the same score. Order of platform events: start → result | error(code) → end; with no result before end the web reports error "no-speech". Error codes the screens react to: not-allowed, service-not-allowed, unsupported, audio-capture, no-speech, network, busy, whisper, phrases-not-supported, language-not-supported.

best.why: the later alternative is closer to the target: the best similarity wins
similarity ignores case, punctuation and anything outside a-z/space
ties keep the FIRST maximum (Array.sort is stable)
blank alternatives are dropped; nothing left ⇒ heard "" and score 0
wrong word, partial credit by edit distance
apostrophes are not letters: removed before comparing
accented letters are not a-z: removed on both sides
a pair shared with lesson.json similarity (heard "don't worry", target "dont worry"): the score must be the same

speak._doc: Speak (web/js/speak/score.js). align(target, heard) = LCS alignment of target words (punctuation kept for display) against heard tokens → [{w, ok}]. score({target,mode,intents,accent}) wraps the platform recognizer: text = ok words / target words, fluency.wpm = round(heard words / seconds · 60) with seconds = max(1, (end||now) − (start||call time))/1000 measured when the result arrives (the end event comes AFTER the result in the real platform, so ms is always 0), conf = platform score/100, unclear = nothing heard, error "unsupported" when no recognizer exists. pass(r) = !unclear && σ(12·text − 9.6) ≥ 0.5 ⇔ text ≥ 0.8 (CAL.calibrated=false: the 80 % target of LEARNING-PATH). The GOP hook (`Gop.score` when r.audio is set) never fires in the web today (r.audio is never set) – there is NO GOP engine in the shipped web (scripts/pron/gop.mjs is a research core), so natives score text only. intentOf: first intent whose keyword (normalised, whole-word) occurs in the heard text.

drill.why: each line has 3 beats: Nghe (listen & repeat) → Nói đuổi (shadow) → Nói từ trí nhớ (first letters only). A passing attempt (Speak.pass: ≥ 80 % words) earns stars: beat 1 or 2 ⇒ 1 star; beat 3 ⇒ 3 stars when said within (words·0.6 + 3) seconds of tapping the mic, else 2. A pass records lines[id] = {best: max(best, text), stars: max(stars, new)}, marks mission tasks whose intents include the line, adds 1 to the week counter (localStorage lk.spk) and rewards {spoken:1, xp: 2·stars}. "Tiếp" (spkNext) is enabled after a pass and moves to the next beat; after beat 3 to the next line; progress pct = round((line·3 + beat + (pass ? 1 : 0)) / (lines·3) · 100)

Data (CONTRASTS, IPA, HOM, NUM, TIPS keys, label keys, SENTENCES, LIGHT, UI.WEAK) is in the content pack (speak-pack.json pron.pairs / pron.coach / consts.weak); randomness is injected: `random` lists the numbers a port must feed in order (cycled).

decide.why: the first alternative that contains exactly ONE of the two words decides (here "sink" ⇒ said the other word)
an alternative with BOTH words is skipped (cannot decide); the next one decides
a spoken digit is normalised to the number word
both words in the same alternative ⇒ cannot decide ⇒ neither
neither word in any alternative ⇒ neither + heard = first alternative
near miss that is neither word
both in different alternatives: the FIRST alternative with exactly one decides
a plain string is accepted as a single alternative
case and punctuation ignored, forms via HOM
blank / null alternatives are filtered out first

sessions.why: no stats: every contrast weight 2 (unpractised); first side chosen by the first random number; sides alternate per contrast; no pair repeated back-to-back
weights = 1 + 3·(1 − accuracy) (2 when unpractised), divided by (1 + used·0.5): the weak contrast "th-s" (20 %) is drawn far more often than "r-l" (90 %)
one contrast: pairs cycle in data order (used % pairs.length), sides alternate
n = 4: a short session of four words

adapt.why: a wrong answer at index i puts the same contrast again at i+3 (another pair of that contrast when one is not already queued after i, same target side), flagged retry:true
index 9 of 10: the retry slot is clamped to the last item; when at ≤ idx nothing changes

stats.why: record: n++ and ok++ when correct; endSession appends {d: day, ok, n} per contrast and keeps the LAST 12; weak = contrasts with n ≥ 2 and accuracy < 0.8, lowest first; acc = ok/n or null

storage.why: stats live in localStorage "lk.pronPairs" (JSON); unreadable or non-object JSON ⇒ {}; saving failure ⇒ false

v.title: Lights Out for Migrants
v.q: Why are 'lights out' programmes attractive to some building managers?

mistakes.answer: C. The programmes reduce the cost of energy.
mistakes.explain: Cuối đoạn E: “Such programmes also save electricity, which makes them attractive to building managers”. “Reduce the cost of energy” = “save electricity” → C. A sai (tình nguyện viên nhặt chim chết, không lau tòa nhà); B (bắt buộc theo luật) và D (truyền thông) không có trong bài.

v.title: Lights Out for Migrants
v.q: What does the writer suggest about early breeding in birds exposed to light?

mistakes.answer: A. It may be harmful because insect food may not yet be plentiful.
mistakes.explain: Đoạn D: “Early breeding may sound like an advantage, but if chicks hatch before the insects they depend on become abundant, many may starve.” “Harmful” = “many may starve”; “insect food may not yet be plentiful” = “before the insects ... become abundant” → A. B trái ý; C (nhiệt độ) không được nêu là nguyên nhân; D sai vì blackbirds/robins chỉ là ví dụ về tiếng hót sớm.

v.title: Lights Out for Migrants
v.q: When are birds at greatest risk in cities?

mistakes.answer: D. when low cloud sends light back towards the ground
mistakes.explain: Đoạn C: “The danger is greatest on cloudy or foggy nights, when ... low cloud reflects the city's light back down towards the ground”. “Greatest risk” = “danger is greatest”; “sends light back towards the ground” = “reflects ... back down towards the ground” → D. A ngược lại (đêm quang đãng); B và C được nhắc đến là mối nguy nhưng không phải lúc nguy hiểm nhất.

v.title: Lights Out for Migrants
v.q: According to paragraph B, what may happen to birds flying over a brightly lit city?

mistakes.answer: B. They use up energy by flying around the city for a long time.
mistakes.explain: Cuối đoạn B: chim bị hút vào vùng sáng và “once inside the glow they may circle for hours, wasting energy they need for the journey”. “Use up energy” = “wasting energy”, “flying around the city for a long time” = “circle for hours” → đáp án B. A sai (ánh sáng gây nhiễu chứ không giúp định vị); C sai (diều hâu không hoạt động ban đêm); D sai (bướm đêm chỉ là phép so sánh).

Describe a teacher who has had a strong.a:
I'd like to talk about Mr Hai, who was my literature teacher in high school. He taught us Vietnamese literature for three years, from grade ten to grade twelve, and I have to say he completely changed the way I looked at the subject.

Before I joined his class, I thought literature was just about learning model essays by heart and repeating them in exams. Mr Hai, however, had a very different approach. He was quite a quiet man, but he had a dry sense of humour and an incredible passion for books. Instead of giving us the answers, he would ask us open-ended questions and let us argue with each other. Sometimes he even played the devil's advocate on purpose, just to see whether we could defend our opinions.

What I remember most clearly is one afternoon when I handed in an essay that I'd basically copied from a guidebook. He didn't scold me in front of the class. Instead, he asked me to stay behind and told me, quite gently, that he wanted to hear my voice, not someone else's. I felt really embarrassed at the time, but that conversation was a real turning point for me.

The reason he influenced me so much is that he taught me to think for myself. From then on, I started reading more widely and writing what I genuinely believed, even if it wasn't the 'safe' answer. That habit has stayed with me ever since, and it has helped me enormously at university, where critical thinking is valued far more than memorisation. Looking back, I'm incredibly grateful that I ended up in his class.
vocab: khiếu hài hước kiểu tỉnh bơ
cố tình phản biện để thử thách lập luận

Should university education be free for.a: I think it's a very appealing idea in principle, because it would give talented young people from poorer backgrounds an equal shot at success. In countries like Germany, free tuition seems to work reasonably well. However, I'm not entirely convinced it's realistic everywhere. Universities are expensive to run, so if students don't pay, taxpayers have to foot the bill, and that money might be needed for schools or hospitals. Perhaps a fairer compromise would be generous scholarships and low-interest loans, so that cost is never the only thing standing between a capable student and a degree.
vocab: một giải pháp dung hòa công bằng hơn

How has technology changed the way stude.a: Quite dramatically, I'd say. The most obvious change is access to information: students no longer have to rely solely on textbooks, because they can watch lectures from top universities or look up almost anything in seconds. Online platforms also let people learn at their own pace, which is great for those who need extra time. On the other hand, there's a downside. Many students get easily distracted by notifications, and some rely on AI tools to do their thinking for them. So technology is a powerful tool, but it really depends on whether students use it wisely.
vocab: học theo tốc độ của riêng mình

What makes a good teacher, in your opini.a: For me, the most important quality is genuine enthusiasm for the subject, because passion tends to be contagious. If a teacher clearly loves what they're teaching, students are far more likely to engage. Beyond that, I think good teachers are patient and can explain difficult ideas in a simple way. A teacher I had at school, for instance, would always use everyday examples to explain abstract concepts in physics. Of course, subject knowledge matters too, but I'd argue that being able to connect with students on a personal level is what really sets great teachers apart.

Is there any technology you could not li.a: I'd have to say my laptop. I know it sounds a bit dramatic, but almost all of my coursework, my notes and even my part-time work are on it. A few months ago it broke down for three days, and I felt completely lost. That experience made me realise just how dependent I've become on it.
vocab: nghe có vẻ hơi phóng đại

Describe a piece of technology that you.a:
The piece of technology I want to talk about is my pair of noise-cancelling headphones. They might sound like a luxury, but honestly, they've become one of the most useful things I own.

I started using them about two years ago, when I moved into a shared flat near my university. The flat was on a busy street, and there was constant noise from motorbikes, street vendors and, to be honest, my flatmates as well. I was finding it almost impossible to focus on my assignments, so after a lot of research, I decided to save up and buy a decent pair. They weren't cheap, but I thought of it as an investment.

These days I use them in all sorts of situations. When I'm studying, I switch on the noise-cancelling mode and listen to some instrumental music, and it's amazing how quickly I can get into a state of deep concentration. I also wear them on long bus journeys, so I can listen to podcasts or English lessons without being bothered by the traffic. And when I need a break, they're perfect for unwinding with my favourite albums.

The main reason they're so useful to me is that they give me control over my environment. Before I had them, I was easily distracted and often stressed, but now I can create my own quiet space wherever I am. My grades actually improved in the semester after I bought them, and I don't think that's a coincidence. Of course, I try not to wear them all the time, because I don't want to shut out the world completely, but overall they've made a huge difference to my productivity and my peace of mind.
vocab: trạng thái tập trung cao độ

Do you think people rely too much on tec.a: To some extent, yes. Many people can't navigate without a map app or remember a single phone number, which suggests we've handed over some basic skills to our devices. I also think constant reliance on smartphones can damage our attention spans. Having said that, I wouldn't call all dependence negative. Technology lets doctors diagnose diseases earlier and allows families to stay connected across continents. So the problem isn't really technology itself, but the lack of balance. If we use it as a tool rather than a crutch, I think the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
vocab: ở một mức độ nào đó
khả năng duy trì sự chú ý

How might artificial intelligence change.a: I think AI is likely to reshape the job market quite significantly. Repetitive tasks, such as data entry or basic customer service, are already being automated, so some of those roles may disappear. On the other hand, new jobs will probably emerge, like people who train, monitor or audit AI systems. Personally, I believe the biggest change will be within existing jobs rather than jobs vanishing altogether. A lawyer or a designer, for example, might use AI to handle routine work and focus on more creative or strategic tasks. The real challenge is making sure workers have the chance to retrain.
vocab: định hình lại thị trường lao động
công việc lặp đi lặp lại

Should children be allowed to use smartp.a: I think it depends largely on the child's age and how the phone is used. For young children, I'd say it's better to delay owning a smartphone, because they can easily become addicted to games or exposed to inappropriate content. For teenagers, though, a phone can be genuinely useful, both for safety and for learning. My younger cousin, for instance, uses hers to look up homework questions and contact her parents. So rather than a complete ban, I'd favour clear rules, like screen-time limits and parental controls, so children learn to use technology responsibly.
vocab: tính năng kiểm soát của phụ huynh

Is there much pollution where you live?.a: Unfortunately, yes. I live in Hanoi, and air pollution has become a serious problem, especially in winter, when the smog can be quite thick. On bad days, I check an air-quality app before going out and wear a mask. Noise pollution is also an issue, because the streets are packed with motorbikes from early morning until late at night.

Do you do anything to protect the enviro.a: I try to do my bit, although I'm far from perfect. For example, I always carry a reusable water bottle and a cloth bag, so I don't need to buy plastic ones. I also separate my rubbish at home. They're small steps, but I think if enough people make these changes, they can really add up.
vocab: cộng dồn lại thành đáng kể

Do you prefer the countryside or the cit.a: At this stage of my life, I'd probably choose the city. There are far more job opportunities, and I love having cafés, cinemas and bookshops on my doorstep. That said, whenever I visit my grandparents in the countryside, I really appreciate the fresh air and the slower pace of life. Maybe I'll move somewhere quieter when I'm older.
vocab: at this stage of my life
ở giai đoạn này của cuộc đời

Describe a natural place you have visite.a:
The place I'd like to describe is Ha Long Bay, in the north-east of Vietnam. It's famous for its thousands of limestone islands rising out of emerald-green water, and it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site, so I'm sure many people have heard of it.

I went there about two summers ago with my family. We'd been planning the trip for months, because it was the first time all of us, including my grandparents, could take time off together. We booked a small boat tour and spent a night on the bay, which turned out to be the highlight of the whole holiday.

During the day, we sailed between the islands, stopped to explore a huge cave full of stalactites, and went kayaking through narrow channels between the rocks. My younger brother and I also tried swimming off the side of the boat, although the water was colder than I expected. In the evening, we sat on the deck, ate fresh seafood and watched the sun go down behind the islands.

The reason it impressed me so much is the sheer scale and beauty of the landscape. Photos really don't do it justice. When you're actually there, surrounded by those towering rocks and complete silence, you feel incredibly small, in a good way. I also remember waking up early the next morning, when there was mist over the water, and it looked almost magical. At the same time, I noticed some plastic floating near the shore, which made me realise how fragile places like this are. So it left me with a sense of wonder, but also a feeling that we need to take better care of them.
vocab: điểm nhấn, phần đáng nhớ nhất
không lột tả hết vẻ đẹp
cảm giác kinh ngạc, thán phục

What are the biggest environmental probl.a: In Vietnam, I'd say the most pressing issue is air pollution in big cities like Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, mainly caused by traffic, construction and industry. Another major problem is plastic waste, which ends up in rivers and eventually the ocean. And of course, as a country with a long coastline, we're particularly vulnerable to climate change. The Mekong Delta, for instance, is already suffering from rising sea levels and saltwater intrusion, which threatens farmers' livelihoods. These problems are interconnected, so I think they need to be tackled together rather than one at a time.

Who should be responsible for protecting.a: I'd argue it has to be a shared responsibility, but governments should take the lead. The truth is that individual actions, like recycling or using less plastic, are important, yet they can only achieve so much. The biggest sources of pollution are usually industries and energy systems, and only governments have the power to regulate them, for example by introducing carbon taxes or investing in public transport. At the same time, policies only work if people actually support them. So ideally, governments set the rules and provide the infrastructure, while individuals change their everyday habits.
vocab: chỉ đạt được đến một mức nhất định

Will renewable energy replace fossil fue.a: I think it will, eventually, but probably not as quickly as many people hope. Solar and wind power have become much cheaper over the last decade, and in some countries they're already the cheapest source of new electricity. However, there are still challenges, such as storing energy for when the sun isn't shining. Many economies are also heavily dependent on coal and oil, so the transition will take time and money. My guess is that fossil fuels will gradually be phased out over the next few decades rather than disappearing overnight.
vocab: chỉ sau một đêm, ngay lập tức

lessons.title: Nguyên âm dài /iː/
lessons.how: Lưỡi nâng cao ở phía trước, đầu lưỡi chạm nhẹ răng dưới. Môi kéo sang hai bên như đang cười, hàm gần khép. Giữ âm dài và căng.
lessons.vn: Người Việt hay đọc ngắn như "i" nên "sheep" nghe thành "ship". Hãy kéo dài gấp đôi và giữ môi căng đến hết âm.
lessons.tip: Giống "i" trong "đi" nhưng kéo dài như khi nói "iii" lúc chụp ảnh.

lessons.title: Âm /θ/ và /ð/ – không phải “th” tiếng Việt
lessons.how: Cả /θ/ và /ð/ đều là âm “giữa hai răng”: đặt đầu lưỡi nhẹ giữa răng trên và răng dưới (hoặc chạm mặt sau răng trên), rồi thổi hơi qua khe hẹp. /θ/ vô thanh – chỉ có hơi (think, health). /ð/ hữu thanh – có rung dây thanh (the, weather). Đây là âm xát kéo dài được, khác hẳn “th” tiếng Việt (một âm tắc bật hơi).
lessons.howEn: English dental fricatives /θ/ (voiceless: think, three) and /ð/ (voiced: this, weather) are produced by resting the tip of the tongue gently between the front teeth (or behind the upper incisors) and pushing a continuous airstream through the constriction without stopping. Unlike Vietnamese “th”, which is an aspirated stop, they are fricatives: the air keeps flowing.

rules.label: /θ/ vô thanh
rules.when: thường ở từ nội dung: danh từ, động từ, số đếm

rules.label: /ð/ hữu thanh
rules.when: thường ở từ chức năng (the, this, that, they, than) và giữa các nguyên âm

rules.label: Danh từ /θ/ → động từ /ð/
rules.when: một số cặp đổi âm khi thành động từ

lessons.vn: Người Việt hay đọc /θ/ thành “th” tiếng Việt hoặc /t/ (“think” → “tink”), hoặc /s/ (“think” → “sink”); đọc /ð/ thành /d/ hoặc /z/ (“they” → “day”, “clothing” → “closing”). Cách sửa: soi gương – phải thấy đầu lưỡi lộ ra giữa hai hàm răng; giữ âm kéo dài “θθθθ” vài giây trước khi nói cả từ.
lessons.tip: Thần chú: “Lè lưỡi – thổi hơi.” Nếu không kéo dài được âm thì bạn đang đọc /t/ hoặc /d/, chưa phải /θ/ /ð/.
lessons.tipEn: Tip: Put the tongue tip lightly between the teeth and let the air flow. If the sound stops like a click, you are saying /t/ or /d/ instead of /θ/ or /ð/.
sentences: I think the growth of the city threatens our health.
Although the weather is warm, they rarely go there.
There are three main methods that I would mention.

quiz.explain: “think” /θɪŋk/ bắt đầu bằng /θ/ vô thanh, lưỡi giữa hai răng, chỉ thổi hơi.
“bathe” /beɪð/ là động từ, kết thúc bằng /ð/. “bath” và “path” kết thúc bằng /θ/.

quiz.q: Nếu đọc /ð/ thành /z/, “clothing” sẽ nghe giống từ nào?
Âm /θ/ khác “th” tiếng Việt ở điểm nào?
options: /θ/ là âm xát, kéo dài được
quiz.explain: “th” tiếng Việt là âm tắc bật hơi. /θ/ là âm xát: hơi đi qua khe giữa lưỡi và răng, có thể kéo dài.

quiz.q: “the” trong câu thường đọc là gì trước phụ âm?
quiz.explain: Trước phụ âm, “the” là dạng yếu /ðə/. Trước nguyên âm thường là /ði/. /də/ là lỗi thay /ð/ bằng /d/.

lessons.title: Trọng âm câu và dạng yếu
lessons.how: Tiếng Anh có nhịp dựa trên trọng âm: các từ mang nội dung (danh từ, động từ chính, tính từ, trạng từ, từ phủ định, từ để hỏi) được nhấn; các từ chức năng (giới từ, mạo từ, trợ động từ, đại từ, liên từ) thường đọc nhanh và nhẹ với nguyên âm /ə/ – gọi là dạng yếu. Khoảng cách giữa các từ được nhấn có xu hướng khá đều nhau, nên các từ yếu bị “nén” lại.
lessons.howEn: In natural spoken English, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs), negatives and question words receive sentence stress, while grammatical function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) are often reduced to weak forms with /ə/ in the middle of a sentence. Stressed words tend to fall at fairly regular intervals, so weak words are squeezed between them. Function words keep strong forms at the end of a clause, when stressed for contrast, and negatives such as can’t are separate words with a full vowel (UK /kɑːnt/, US /kænt/). Saying every word with a full vowel makes speech sound stiff and robotic.

rules.label: Từ được nhấn
rules.when: danh từ, động từ chính, tính từ, trạng từ, not/never, từ để hỏi

rules.label: Dạng yếu
rules.when: giới từ, mạo từ, trợ động từ, liên từ khi đứng giữa câu

rules.label: Dạng mạnh
rules.when: khi đứng cuối câu hoặc được nhấn đối lập; “can’t” là từ riêng với nguyên âm đầy đủ

lessons.vn: Người Việt đọc mọi từ to và rõ như nhau (“I – WANT – TO – GO – TO – THE – PARK”), làm câu nghe “cứng như robot” và giám khảo khó nhận ra từ khóa. Đặc biệt nguy hiểm: “can” đọc mạnh /kæn/ dễ bị nghe thành “can't”. Cách sửa: gạch chân từ nội dung, đọc to chúng trước, sau đó “chèn” các từ yếu vào giữa thật nhanh mà giữ nguyên nhịp.
lessons.tip: Thần chú: “Nội dung thì nhấn – chức năng thì lướt.” Khi không nhấn, “can” khẳng định là /kən/, còn “can't” là /kɑːnt/ (giọng Mỹ: /kænt/) – nguyên âm khác hẳn.
lessons.tipEn: Tip: Stress the content, glide over the grammar. Positive “can” is usually /kən/, whereas “can’t” keeps a full vowel: /kɑːnt/ in British English, /kænt/ in American English.

PEOple can SAVE a LOT of MONey by COOKing at HOME. ↘
MOST of my FRIENDS are INterested in techNOlogy. ↘

quiz.q: Từ nào thường ĐƯỢC NHẤN trong câu?
quiz.explain: “pollution” là danh từ – từ nội dung. “the” và “and” là từ chức năng, thường đọc yếu.

quiz.q: Câu “I can swim” trong giọng Anh, “can” đọc là?
quiz.explain: Khẳng định, giữa câu → /kən/, và nhấn vào “SWIM”. “can't” mới là /kɑːnt/.

th-s: Thè đầu lưỡi ra giữa hai hàm răng rồi thổi hơi nhẹ – không để lưỡi sau răng.
Giữ đầu lưỡi sau răng trên, không thè ra; xì hơi như tiếng rắn “sss”.
th-t: Thè đầu lưỡi ra giữa hai hàm răng rồi thổi hơi nhẹ – không để lưỡi sau răng.
Chạm đầu lưỡi vào lợi sau răng trên rồi bật ra – không thè lưỡi.
dh-d: Thè đầu lưỡi giữa hai hàm răng, thổi hơi và rung cổ (đặt tay lên cổ để cảm nhận).
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi sau răng trên rồi bật ra, có rung cổ – không thè lưỡi.
dh-z: Thè đầu lưỡi giữa hai hàm răng, thổi hơi và rung cổ (đặt tay lên cổ để cảm nhận).
Giữ lưỡi sau răng và ngân “zzz” như tiếng ong – không thè lưỡi.
s-z: Âm cuối /s/ không rung cổ và nguyên âm trước nó ngắn: “rice” gọn, xì hơi rõ.
Âm cuối /z/ rung cổ và kéo dài nguyên âm trước nó: “riiise-zzz”.
final-drop: Đừng nuốt âm cuối: chặn rồi bật nhẹ /t/, /k/, /p/, /d/ ở cuối từ.
Từ này kết thúc bằng nguyên âm – không thêm phụ âm cuối, kéo dài nguyên âm tự nhiên.
final-voice: Phụ âm cuối vô thanh: cắt nguyên âm ngắn rồi bật hơi gọn /t/ /k/ /f/.
Phụ âm cuối hữu thanh: kéo dài nguyên âm và rung cổ khi kết thúc /d/ /ɡ/ /v/.
p-b: Cuối từ /p/: khép môi, nguyên âm ngắn, bật hơi nhẹ – không rung cổ.
Cuối từ /b/: nguyên âm dài hơn, khép môi và rung cổ – đừng đọc thành “p”.
plural: Từ này ở dạng số ít – dừng sau phụ âm cuối, không thêm /s/.
Đừng bỏ đuôi -s: đọc rõ /s/, /z/ hoặc /ɪz/ ở cuối từ.
ed: Đây là dạng nguyên mẫu – kết thúc gọn, không thêm âm /t/ hay /d/.
Đọc rõ đuôi -ed: /t/ sau âm vô thanh, /d/ sau âm hữu thanh, /ɪd/ sau t, d.
sh-s: Chu môi tròn ra trước, lưỡi lùi về sau một chút, thổi “suỵt” /ʃ/.
Môi dẹt, đầu lưỡi sát răng trên, xì hơi mảnh “sss” – không chu môi.
ch-sh: Bắt đầu bằng một cú chặn /t/ rồi bật ra “ch” – âm ngắn, dứt khoát.
Không chặn lưỡi: để hơi chảy liên tục “shhh”.
ch-j: Như “ch” nhưng không rung cổ – chỉ bật hơi.
Cùng khẩu hình với “ch” nhưng rung cổ: “j” trong “jeep”.
j-z: Chặn lưỡi rồi bật ra “dʒ” có rung cổ – môi hơi chu.
Không chặn: lưỡi sau răng, ngân liên tục “zzz”.
j-y: Âm “j” có chặn lưỡi và rung cổ, mạnh hơn “y”.
Âm /j/ nhẹ, lướt nhanh như “i” ngắn – lưỡi không chạm ngạc.
r-l: Cong đầu lưỡi lên nhưng KHÔNG chạm ngạc, môi hơi tròn.
Đầu lưỡi chạm chắc vào lợi sau răng trên, hơi đi hai bên lưỡi.
l-n: Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi nhưng hơi đi qua miệng – không phải qua mũi.
Đầu lưỡi chạm lợi và hơi đi qua mũi (bịt mũi sẽ thấy khác).
cluster: Đọc liền cụm phụ âm, không chèn “ơ” vào giữa: “sport”, không phải “sơ-port”.
Từ này có thêm một âm tiết nhẹ /ə/ – đọc rõ hai âm tiết.
i-ih: Kéo môi cười, căng lưỡi và kéo dài “iiii”.
Thả lỏng miệng, đọc ngắn và gọn – giữa “i” và “ê”.
ae-e: Há miệng rộng, hạ cằm xuống thấp như “e” kéo về “a”.
Miệng mở vừa, cằm không hạ sâu – “e” gọn.
uh-ah: Miệng mở vừa, thả lỏng, âm ngắn như “â”.
Há miệng thật to, lưỡi hạ thấp, kéo dài “aaa” như khi bác sĩ khám họng.
v-b: Răng trên chạm nhẹ môi dưới, thổi hơi và rung cổ – môi không khép lại.
Hai môi khép chặt rồi bật ra – răng không chạm môi.

passages.title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper
passages.titleVi: Sự trở lại của nghề nuôi ong đô thị

paras.t: On the flat roofs of office blocks, hotels and apartment buildings in many of the world's large cities, a quiet agricultural revival has been taking place. Wooden hives, painted white or pale green, now sit beside air-conditioning units and satellite dishes, and in summer the air above them is busy with honeybees. Urban beekeeping is not new – city dwellers kept bees in gardens and backyards for centuries – but the practice declined sharply during the twentieth century as cities grew denser and local regulations discouraged keeping livestock of any kind close to homes. Since the early 2000s, however, the number of registered hives in several European and North American cities has risen dramatically, and in some districts it has more than tripled within a decade.

Several forces lie behind this revival. The most widely cited is public concern about the decline of pollinators. Reports of colony losses in the countryside, linked to pesticides, disease and the loss of wild flowers, were widely covered in the media, and many people concluded that they could help by keeping bees themselves. At the same time, a broader interest in locally produced food encouraged restaurants and hotels to install hives so that they could serve honey made only a few metres from the kitchen. For businesses, a rooftop hive also became a visible symbol of environmental responsibility, often featured in annual reports and marketing material.

Surprisingly, cities can be good places for bees. Urban areas are often warmer than the surrounding countryside, which extends the season during which flowers bloom and bees can forage. Parks, private gardens, street trees, railway embankments and cemeteries provide a wide variety of plants, and because these are planted for decoration rather than for crops, they flower at different times of the year. In contrast, large farms may offer a single crop that blooms intensely for two or three weeks and then leaves bees with almost nothing. Cities also tend to use fewer agricultural chemicals, although garden pesticides remain a concern. Some beekeepers report that their city colonies produce more honey per hive than those they keep in rural areas.

Nevertheless, scientists have begun to warn that the enthusiasm for rooftop hives may be causing problems of its own. The honeybee is a single, domesticated species, but most pollination in the wild is carried out by thousands of species of wild bees, together with hoverflies, moths and butterflies. A study carried out in one large European capital found that in districts with the highest density of hives, wild bee numbers had fallen over a ten-year period, while in districts with few hives they had remained stable. The researchers suggested that honeybees, which live in colonies of tens of thousands, were simply outcompeting smaller wild species for the limited supply of nectar and pollen. In other words, adding hives does not necessarily help pollinators in general; it may help one species at the expense of others.

Disease is another worry. When hives are placed close together, infections such as viruses and parasitic mites can pass more easily from colony to colony, and there is some evidence that they can also spread to wild bees visiting the same flowers. Experienced beekeepers inspect their hives regularly and treat infections, but the rapid growth in the hobby has brought in many newcomers who lack the necessary skills. In one survey of urban beekeepers, almost a third admitted that they had not checked their colonies for mites during the previous year.

In response, some city authorities and beekeeping associations have changed their approach. Rather than encouraging every company to place a hive on its roof, they now advise people who want to help bees to plant more flowers instead. A small number of cities have introduced a registration scheme, so that officials can track how many colonies exist in each neighbourhood and identify areas where numbers may be too high. Training courses, often run by local associations, have become a requirement for membership in some places, and new beekeepers are encouraged to work alongside a mentor for their first season.

The future of urban beekeeping is therefore likely to be more carefully managed than its recent past. Supporters argue that hives still have a valuable role: they connect city residents with nature, offer educational opportunities for schools, and produce honey with flavours that reflect the particular mix of plants in each neighbourhood. Critics accept these benefits but insist that the real measure of success should be the health of all pollinators, not the number of hives. Both sides agree on one point: a city that wants to support bees must first provide enough food for them, and that means more trees, more flowering plants and fewer neatly mown lawns.

passages.title: Does Testing Make Schools Better?
passages.titleVi: Thi cử chuẩn hóa có giúp trường học tốt hơn?

paras.t: Few policies in modern education have generated as much heat as the standardised test. To its supporters, a common examination taken by every pupil at a given age is the only fair way to discover whether schools are doing their job; to its critics, it is a blunt instrument that narrows teaching, demoralises teachers and reveals little that a good teacher did not already know. Both camps tend to present the question as a simple choice between accountability and freedom. I want to argue that this framing is mistaken, and that the real issue is not whether we test but what we do with the results.

The case for testing begins with a problem of information. Before national assessments were introduced in many countries, parents and governments had remarkably little reliable knowledge about how well children in different schools were learning. Inspections took place infrequently, and a school's reputation often reflected the social background of its pupils rather than the quality of its teaching. The economist Helena Marchetti, in her analysis of school records from three countries, found that once results were published, the gap between the highest- and lowest-performing schools serving similar communities narrowed noticeably over the following decade. Her interpretation is that publication exposed weak schools that had previously escaped attention, and that local authorities then directed support towards them. This seems to me a genuine achievement, and one that critics of testing too rarely acknowledge.

Yet the same evidence can be read another way. Tobias Lindqvist, a sociologist who interviewed teachers in schools that had improved their scores rapidly, discovered that much of the improvement came from intensive preparation for the specific format of the test rather than from deeper learning. When pupils from these schools sat a different examination covering the same subjects, their advantage largely disappeared. This phenomenon – sometimes called 'score inflation' – is perhaps the most serious objection to high-stakes testing. When a number is used to reward or punish, people will find ways to raise the number, and not all of those ways involve better education.

A related concern is the narrowing of the curriculum. If only reading and mathematics are tested, there is an obvious temptation to reduce the time spent on music, art, history or physical education. Amara Okafor's survey of primary head teachers found that more than half had cut time from untested subjects in the year before an important assessment. Defenders of testing sometimes reply that literacy and numeracy are the foundation of all other learning, so that concentrating on them is no bad thing. There is some truth in this, but it overlooks the fact that children often acquire reading skills through the content of other subjects; a child who reads widely about history or science may become a better reader than one who practises comprehension exercises alone.

It is also frequently claimed that testing damages pupils' well-being. Here, I think, the evidence is weaker than either side admits. Rafael Duarte, a psychologist, measured anxiety levels among eleven-year-olds before and after national examinations and found that while a minority experienced considerable stress, the majority reported only mild nervousness, comparable to what they felt before a school sports competition. Crucially, the pupils who were most anxious were those whose teachers talked most about the consequences of the results for the school. This suggests that the stress comes less from the tests themselves than from the pressure that adults attach to them.

What, then, should policymakers conclude? The most persuasive research, in my view, is that which looks at how test results are used rather than whether they exist. Ingrid Solberg compared education systems that use national tests mainly for diagnosis – identifying which pupils and schools need extra help – with systems in which results determine teachers' pay or even a school's survival. She found that the diagnostic systems achieved similar gains in pupil learning while producing far less score inflation and curriculum narrowing. When the stakes are lowered, in other words, the information that tests provide becomes more trustworthy, precisely because there is less incentive to manipulate it.

None of this means that testing is harmless or that its critics are simply defending the comfort of teachers. But the debate would be more productive if both sides recognised that a test is a measuring tool, and that a tool can be used well or badly. A thermometer does not cure a fever, but a doctor without one would be working in the dark. The question for the coming decade is not whether schools should be measured, but whether we can design systems in which measurement informs improvement instead of replacing it.

passages.title: Lights Out for Migrants
passages.titleVi: Tắt đèn vì chim di cư

paras.t: For most of human history, the night sky above a town was almost as dark as the sky above a forest. That is no longer the case. Satellite images show that the area of the Earth's surface lit artificially at night has grown by roughly two per cent a year in recent decades, and in many regions the glow of a large city can be seen from more than a hundred kilometres away. Astronomers were among the first to complain about this 'light pollution', since it hides faint stars from their telescopes. Over the past thirty years, however, biologists have come to regard artificial light at night as a serious environmental issue in its own right, comparable in some respects to noise or chemical pollution.

Among the animals most affected are migratory birds. A large proportion of the songbird species that migrate between Europe and Africa, or between North and South America, travel at night. Flying in darkness offers several advantages: the air is cooler and calmer, predators such as hawks are inactive, and the daylight hours can be spent feeding. To find their way, these birds rely on a combination of cues, including the position of the stars, the Earth's magnetic field and the pattern of light visible at sunset. Artificial light interferes with this system. Birds flying over a brightly lit city are drawn towards it, in much the same way that moths are attracted to a lamp, and once inside the glow they may circle for hours, wasting energy they need for the journey.

The consequences can be fatal. Exhausted birds land in unsuitable places such as car parks and courtyards, where there is little food and many dangers, including cats. Others collide with glass buildings, which either reflect the sky or allow the bird to see vegetation on the other side. Estimates of the number of birds killed by collisions with buildings each year vary widely, but even cautious figures run into hundreds of millions worldwide. The danger is greatest on cloudy or foggy nights, when the stars are hidden and low cloud reflects the city's light back down towards the ground, creating a bright dome in which birds become trapped.

Light also alters the behaviour of birds that live permanently in cities. Researchers in several countries have found that urban blackbirds and robins begin singing earlier in the morning than their rural relatives, sometimes several hours before dawn. One study, which compared birds nesting in dark woodland with birds nesting close to street lamps, found that the birds exposed to light started breeding up to a month earlier in spring. Early breeding may sound like an advantage, but if chicks hatch before the insects they depend on become abundant, many may starve. The same light that affects birds disrupts insects too: a single street lamp can attract and kill large numbers of moths on a summer night, reducing the food available for bats and birds and the number of insects available to pollinate night-flowering plants.

The encouraging aspect of light pollution, compared with many other environmental problems, is that it can be reversed almost immediately. Once a light is switched off, its effect disappears. Several cities on major migration routes have launched 'lights out' programmes, asking the owners of tall buildings to turn off or dim unnecessary lighting during the peak weeks of spring and autumn migration. In one city, volunteers who collected dead and injured birds from the streets every morning found that collisions fell by more than half at buildings that took part. Such programmes also save electricity, which makes them attractive to building managers who might otherwise be reluctant to change their routines.

Engineers and designers are also changing how outdoor light is produced. Fully shielded fixtures direct light downwards onto the street, rather than allowing it to escape sideways or upwards into the sky. Motion sensors ensure that lights in car parks and on footpaths are on only when someone is present. The colour of the light matters as well. The bright white LEDs that have replaced older orange street lamps in many cities contain a large proportion of blue light, which is particularly disruptive to wildlife and to human sleep. Warmer, amber-coloured LEDs appear to affect animals far less, while still allowing people to see clearly. However, specialists warn that because LEDs are so cheap to run, cities may simply install more of them, so that any benefit is cancelled out by the increase in the total amount of light. Technology alone, they argue, cannot replace the simple decision to use less light.
